1477	- A missing reference target is reported instead of emitting a broken link.
1478	- Unsupported metadata is reported instead of being claimed as enforced.
1479	- Generated files are tracked in `.piton/manifest.json`, so cleanup never
1480	  deletes files users wrote. Its `targets` records, for each target, the
1481	  documentation date the generated files were validated against.
1482	- Failures name the source anchor and property. Output stays inside its
1483	  configured boundaries.
1484	
1485	### 11.7 Open decisions
1486	
1487	`spec/scope/belay/Decisions.pi` lists what is not decided. Tooling should say
1488	it is unspecified rather than guess:
1489	
1490	- Placement of instructions outside `shapeRoot`.
1491	- The types of `tools`, `allowed-tools` and `model`, and their mapping per
1492	  adapter.
1493	- Naming: skill filename normalization, command name normalization before the
1494	  `x-` prefix, acronym splitting and collision handling.
1495	- Whether workflows stay compositions of the four constructs. Do not add a
1496	  `workflow` keyword just because examples describe agent processes.
1497	- How platform-specific adapter options are written.
1498	
1499	Do not present any of these as settled. If your work depends on one, raise it
1500	with the user.
1501	
1502	## 12. Package management
1503	
1504	Packages are git repositories, managed as **vendored dependencies**. Installed
1505	packages are stored inside the project and committed to version control, and
1506	the tooling adds, updates, removes and inspects them. Nothing is fetched at
1507	compile time.
1508	
1509	- **Offering packages.** A repository declares packages with `piton-package`
1510	  anchors (`PitonPackage` from `@piton/packaging`: `name`, `root`,
1511	  `dependencies`). A package anchor can live anywhere in the specbase but must
1512	  be listed under `packages:` in `piton.config.pi`. A package's `root` is
1513	  relative to `piton.config.pi`, like the project's own root. **`packages:` is what the
1514	  repository offers to other projects; a project never installs its own
1515	  packages.** One repository can offer several packages, each with its own
1516	  root and dependencies.
1517	- **Names.** `name` is what the package installs under. It exists because it
1518	  can be kebab-case (`my-package`), which an anchor name can't. Left out, the
1519	  anchor's own name is used. **Package names are flat: no `/`.** Names like
1520	  `@piton/belay` are only for the packages bundled with the compiler.
1521	- **Dependencies.** `dependencies:` lists git URLs, each with an optional
1522	  `commit:`, `tag:` or `branch:` on an indented line beneath it (a dictionary
1523	  item right after the URL). **Only one pin per URL**; more is
1524	  `multiple-pins`. Without a pin, the latest commit on the default branch is
1525	  used. **Pins are strings**: `@piton/config` types them as strings, so
1526	  `tag: 1.0` stays `"1.0"`. Other pin diagnostics are `dangling-pin` and
1527	  `unknown-pin`.
1528	- **Picking packages.** A repository can offer several packages. You get all
1529	  of them unless you list the ones you want with `packages:` under the URL:
1530	  `packages: [ui-kit]`.
1531	- **Project and package dependencies are separate.** The project's apply only
1532	  to the project, and each package declares its own.
1533	- **No nested dependencies.** When two packages need the same package at
1534	  different versions, **the one with the newest commit wins** and a warning is
1535	  shown.
1536	- **Installation.** Each package goes into `tethers/<name>`, next to
1537	  `piton.config.pi`, with the files from its `root`. A repository offering
1538	  `ui-kit` and `my-package` gives `tethers/ui-kit` and `tethers/my-package`.
1539	  Tethering removes every trace of git. A repository that offers no packages
1540	  is installed whole, under the name its URL implies.
1541	- **Importing.** An installed package is a location placeholder:
1542	  `from my-package import X`, `use my-package`, `use my-package/MyAnchor`.
1543	  Normal path resolution applies below it. A missing package is a compiler
1544	  error.
1545	- **Lock file.** `.piton/tether.lock`, next to `piton.config.pi`, keeps each
1546	  tethered package's URL, commit and a hash of its files. `tether` and
1547	  `update` write it, and it is committed with the project.
1548	- **Conflicts.** Before tether, update or any other operation on an installed
1549	  package, the tooling compares its files with the lock file and goes ahead
1550	  only if nothing changed. If the files were edited, it says so and asks the
1551	  user to untether (or `piton update --force` to discard the edits).
1552	
1553	The commands:
1554	
1555	- `piton tether` on its own installs everything in `dependencies`. Given a
1556	  source URL, it adds it to `dependencies` in `piton.config.pi` and installs
1557	  it. `--as <name>` installs under another name.
1558	- `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` reinstalls from
1559	  `dependencies`, all packages when none are named. `--force` replaces a
1560	  package even if it was edited, discarding the edits with a warning;
1561	  `--diff` prints a coloured unified diff of every file each update changed.
1562	- `piton untether <package>` moves the package from `tethers/` to
1563	  `<root>/untethered/` and rewrites the imports that named it, making it the
1564	  project's own source. `--as <name>` renames it; `--no-rewrite` only moves
1565	  it.
1566	- `piton remove <package>` deletes an installed package and removes it from
1567	  `dependencies`. It refuses if the files were edited or if anything still
1568	  imports the package.
1569	
1570	## 13. CLI reference
1571	
1572	Every command prints what it produced first, then a one-line outcome (✓ or
1573	✗), and its problems last: diagnostics, errors and warnings with their help
1574	and notes, then the error and warning count. On a terminal the output is
1575	coloured and paths are marked `+`/`-`; piped or with `NO_COLOR`, it is plain
1576	text and stdout carries the bare results.
1577	
1578	| Command | Behaviour |
1579	| --- | --- |
1580	| `piton check [paths...]` | Validates syntax, imports, references, types, inheritance, composition, exports and circular dependencies, reporting errors and warnings. Writes nothing. Exits 0 when there are no errors and 1 otherwise. Paths are optional files, directories or globs; the default is the project (or every `.pi` file under the working directory when there's no `piton.config.pi`). |
1581	| `piton build [config] [--dry-run]` | Builds the project configured by `piton.config.pi` (or the given config). Writes renderer output to `<output>/<path under root>.<ext>` (defaults: `./dist`, JSON), so `spec/components/Button.pi` becomes `dist/components/Button.json`: the entry file plus every file holding something the entry's exports reference. A registered framework's output replaces it unless the config sets `output` or `renderer`, which asks for both. Records every file in `.piton/manifest.json`. The whole plan is validated before anything is written. `--dry-run` reports without writing. |
1582	| `piton compile <path> [--renderer json\|yaml\|markdown] [--write] [--dependencies]` | Compiles one file to stdout (JSON by default): one key per export. `--write` writes `<file>.<ext>` next to each input and is required for globs. `--dependencies` wraps the result as `{"value": "<compiled output as a string>", "dependencies": [absolute source paths]}` so build tools know what to watch; bundled package files are left out. |
1583	| `piton format [path] [--check]` | Applies canonical formatting (4-space indents, constraint spacing, sorted and wrapped imports, no `.pi` in import paths, a space after `//`). `--check` reports without writing. `piton format -` reads source from stdin and writes the formatted text to stdout. It **only splits overflowing lines and never rejoins a paragraph**, so rewrap edited prose by hand, and don't reflow `key: value` blocks as prose. |
1584	| `piton reach [targets...] [--no-unreachable] [--no-paths]` | Starting from files, globs or anchor names (the entry by default), follows outgoing imports, references, inheritance and composition, direct and transitive. Reports what is reachable with its depth and the path taken, and what is unreachable. The flags hide the last two. Use it to find dead spec. Grouped by source, with a summary. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
1585	| `piton slice <target> [--adapter <target>]` | Prints the part of the spec one thing depends on, as one Markdown document for an agent's prompt. The target is `file.pi#Anchor`, `file.pi#Anchor.property`, `file.pi#variable`, or a bare name looked up across the project (an error when more than one file declares it). Follows, transitively: what an anchor extends, every base that also declares a property, anchors named by type constraints, what a value read (`${Other.x}`, variables), and what it references or embeds. Imports alone bring nothing in. A whole anchor needs all its properties and bases; slicing a property leaves out the anchor's other properties; a reference to a property needs only that property. It also includes the **chain** from the project's entry down to the target (`Specification.Tooling`, `Tooling.cli`, `Cli.commands`): the shortest path the build takes, each link only that one property and not followed further. An export of the entry, a variable, and a file the build doesn't reach have no chain. Order: the target, then its dependencies nearest first (source order breaks ties), then the chain outermost first, so the same source prints the same bytes. Each declaration appears once, headed by its name as written (`SaveButton.color`), with its file, what it extends, its type and what it reads. References and embeds are written as names; cycles are followed until they come back around. Every path it prints is relative to the directory it runs in, and it finds the project by looking upward for `piton.config.pi`. `--adapter claude-code` (any Belay target the project builds) cites the compiled output instead: each location and every reference links to where `piton build` writes it (an embedded anchor to the section that embeds it), and no `.pi` file is ever cited; an abstract base or an anchor that is only read has no document of its own and is described without one. With `--adapter` the target itself must be something the build writes out. Markdown links the author wrote pass through unchanged. Exits 1 on errors. |
1586	| `piton init [directory] [--template <group/name>] [--adapter <id>...] [--list]` | Starts a new project from a template compiled into the compiler (no network needed). Templates come in groups: `piton/minimal` (plain Piton to JSON), `piton/library` (a package others can tether), `belay/application` (a shape instruction placed in `src/`, a skill, an agent and a command) and `belay/minimal` (the Belay config and one skill). Without a directory it first asks for the project's name and creates that directory (an empty answer, or no terminal, uses the working one). Then it asks for a group and a template (`--template belay` asks only for the template), and for a Belay template, which adapters to build for: a checklist of Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode with the template's default (Claude Code) checked, or `--adapter`, repeated or comma-separated. The chosen adapters replace the config's import and `adapters` list, and a template's `.adapters/<id>/` files (like OpenCode's `opencode.json`) are written only for the adapters chosen. Templates are the `group/name` directories in the compiler repo's `create-templates/`, each with a one-line `.template` description that is not written out; adding one is adding a directory, and every template must check cleanly, be formatted, and build. `--list` describes the groups and templates and does nothing else. With no terminal, a full template name is required. It never overwrites a file: if any it would write exists, it names each and writes none, and cancelling a question writes nothing. Prints each written path on stdout, then a summary and the next commands on stderr. Exits 1 on errors. |
1587	| `piton loc [paths...]` | Counts total, code, comment and blank lines per file, with a summary. Defaults to the project. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
1588	| `piton lsp` | Runs the language server over stdio (section 14). |
1589	| `piton agent [claude] [--print-fluency] [args...]` | Launches the agent with a short project primer plus this fluency prompt (the project's `FLUENCY_PROMPT.md`, or the copy built into the compiler), passed to `claude` as `--append-system-prompt`. Extra arguments go to the agent. `--print-fluency` prints the prompt and does nothing else. |
1590	| `piton tether [source] [--as name]` | See section 12. |
1591	| `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` | See section 12. |
1592	| `piton untether <package> [--as name] [--no-rewrite]` | See section 12. |
1593	| `piton remove <package>` | See section 12. |
1594	
1595	Each CLI command in the spec is a `cli-command` anchor
1596	(`spec/scope/tooling/cli/index.pi`) with `commandName`, `positionalArguments`
1597	and `namedArguments`.
1598	
1599	## 14. Language server, editors, and JavaScript
1600	
1601	`piton lsp` provides, from the spec's feature list:
1602	
1603	- Diagnostics (not for missing optional properties), completion, hover (type,
1604	  source, documentation, inheritance chain, export status and compiled
1605	  interpretation), go-to-definition, find-references, and rename across the
1606	  whole specbase.
1607	- Auto-import, import organization, and code actions: import a missing
1608	  symbol, create an unresolved anchor, add an export, qualify an ambiguous
1609	  reference, resolve a simple inheritance conflict.
1610	- Document and workspace symbols, semantic highlighting, inlay hints
1611	  (resolved types, inherited origins, composition sources), formatting,
1612	  folding and selection ranges.
1613	- Inheritance, composition (`+`, `++`), override and conflict resolution;
1614	  reference resolution; validation and type information for expressions in
1615	  `{}`, `${}`, `#{}` and `@{}`; export validation; module resolution; cycle
1616	  detection (circular imports are fine and not reported).
1617	- Related-symbol navigation, a hierarchy view, resolved-value and provenance
1618	  inspection, compiled-output preview, source-to-output mapping, unused and
1619	  redundant definition detection, and documentation integration.
1620	- Incremental analysis and workspace indexing.
1621	- Diagnostics cover Belay semantics as well as Piton. Import organization
1622	  flags unused, duplicate, invalid and overly broad imports. Cycle detection
1623	  also catches an anchor that ends up extending itself, and shows the cycle.
1624	
1625	There is no signature help.
1626	
1627	Completion rules: never suggest things that don't exist; offer nothing on an
1628	empty value (`property: `), because prose probably follows; offer nothing
1629	after a `.` inside a string.
1630	
1631	Editing rules every editor must follow, through the LSP or the editor
1632	extension:
1633	
1634	- Enter after a colon that opens a dictionary or anchor property starts a new
1635	  line indented one level deeper.
1636	- Enter on a blank line inside a dictionary or anchor starts a new line one
1637	  level shallower.
1638	- Format-on-save is optional. It adds the space after `//` and touches nothing
1639	  else that is commented.
1640	
1641	Supported editors and their highlighters (spec): VS Code (TextMate plus LSP);
1642	Emacs, Helix and Zed (tree-sitter plus LSP); Neovim and Vim (vim syntax);
1643	JetBrains (`jetbrains`); Sublime (sublime-syntax); Kate (KSyntaxHighlighting).
1644	Every editor gets full LSP support. The integrations live under `editors/`.
1645	
1646	**Consuming Piton from JavaScript.** `packages/vite-plugin-piton` imports
1647	`.pi` files as modules, with HMR, dependency tracking (through
1648	`piton compile --dependencies`) and virtual modules. Each export in the Piton
1649	file is a named export, and the default export is the whole file, the same as
1650	`piton compile` gives:
1651	
1652	```ts
1653	import { SaveButton } from '../spec/app.pi';
1654	import spec from '../spec/app.pi';
1655	
1656	const button = SaveButton;
1657	const cancel = spec.CancelButton;
1658	```
1659	
1660	It has a configurable default renderer (`renderer: 'json' | 'yaml' |
1661	'markdown'`), and the renderers can also be imported as functions
1662	(`vite-plugin-piton/renderers`) and used inline. `packages/astro-piton` is an
1663	Astro integration that wraps the Vite plugin.
1664	
1665	## 15. Working on a specbase
1666	
1667	1. **Orient.** Open `piton.config.pi` to find `root`, `entry`, `output`, the
1668	   frameworks, the adapters, `codeRoot` and `shapeRoot`. Read the entry file,
1669	   usually `spec/index.pi`, because its exports are the compilation roots.
1670	   Follow the `index.pi` files down through the modules. In this repository,
1671	   `spec/index.pi` exports `Specification` (FoundingThesis, Language, Tooling,
1672	   Belay, PackageManagement) plus the skills and command in `spec/agent/`.
1673	2. **Read compiled reference for overview, and source for truth.**
1674	   `<referenceRoot>/**/*.md` is easy to browse, and its links are lazy, so
1675	   follow them only when relevant.
1676	3. **Edit the `.pi` source**, following the conventions around it:
1677	   - one exported anchor per file, named after the file;
1678	   - `index.pi` files that re-export with `from ./X export *`;
1679	   - abstract anchors exported with a keyword, and shared abstracts in a
1680	     `lib/` folder;
1681	   - lowerCamelCase property names;
1682	   - SCREAMING_CASE for exported constant lists;
1683	   - prose in string blocks, and structure in keys and lists;
1684	   - `@{X}` to link related documents;
1685	   - examples inside fences wrapped in a `\\\` escape block.
1686	4. **Keep imports honest.** Use `use` for keywords and `from ... import` for
1687	   names; a file often needs both. A new file only compiles if the entry
1688	   reaches it, so export it through an index or reference it.
1689	5. **Validate.**
1690	   - Run `piton check`.
1691	   - `piton check` does **not** compile the examples inside escape blocks
1692	     (they are literal text). When you edit spec examples, extract each ` ```piton ` block,
1693	     run `piton compile` on it, and compare with any ` ```json ` block that
1694	     follows. Remember that compile output has only exported names.
1695	   - Run `piton build`, then look at the diff of the generated files.
1696	   - Run `piton reach` to confirm new anchors are reached.
1697	   - Run `piton format --check`.
1698	6. **Never hand-edit generated files.** That includes `CLAUDE.md` and
1699	   `AGENTS.md` under `codeRoot`, everything under `.claude/`, `.codex/`,
1700	   `.agents/`, `.opencode/` and the build output directory that is listed in
1701	   `.piton/manifest.json`, and the files in `.piton/` themselves.
1702	7. **Keep implementation and spec in agreement.** The implementation is judged
1703	   against the spec. When they disagree, report it instead of quietly bending
1704	   the spec to fit. Trust `piton compile` for how things behave today, and
1705	   flag the gap.
1706	
1707	## 16. Where the compiler differs from the spec
1708	
1709	Checked with `piton compile` and `piton build`:
1710	
1711	- The CLI has a few things the spec doesn't name: `build --dry-run`,
1712	  `tether --as`, agent argument passthrough, the `reach` flags, and
1713	  `format` with no path or `-`.
1714	
1715	- **Paragraph breaks.** The spec says a blank line in a string block starts a
1716	  new paragraph. The compiler joins the paragraphs with a single `\n`, which
1717	  Markdown output renders as one paragraph with a soft line break.
1718	
1719	Known limitations, where the spec is silent and the compiler's choice may
1720	surprise you:
1721	
1722	- A `/`-rooted import inside an installed package resolves against the
1723	  consuming project's root, not the package's. Use relative imports inside a
1724	  package.
1725	- A required property from an abstract is not satisfied by a value inherited
1726	  from a concrete base (`needs Thing extends Base`, where `Base` supplies it):
1727	  the keyword's anchor comes last, and its value-less declaration wins. Give
1728	  the value on the anchor itself.
1729	- `piton check` with no paths checks what the entry reaches, so a file that
1730	  nothing imports is not checked. Name it: `piton check path/to/file.pi`.
1731	- **Prose directly in an anchor body is silently dropped.** `anchor A:` with
1732	  only a line of text under it (no key) compiles to an empty anchor, with no
1733	  diagnostic. Always put prose under a key, such as `description:`.
1734	- Mixed-type equality is simply unequal: `{1 == "1"}` is `false`, not an
1735	  error. The spec says `==` works on every type but doesn't spell this out.
1736	- Which constructs each adapter requires a `description` for (section 11.2)
1737	  is hardcoded in `crates/piton-belay/src/adapter.rs`, not declared in the
1738	  adapter `.pi` files.

# Harness Integration Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

Uses the one-off version of a coding harness for the selected ProjectDirectoryScope: `claude -p`, `codex exec`, or `opencode run`, whichever the user chose. Each run carries on a conversation, so the harness keeps its context between requests.

### Shape

#### Description

Should always run in auto mode.
The compiled systemPrompt of a prompt's hidden anchor is appended to the harness's own system prompt, for example with `--append-system-prompt`.
The prompt is given to the harness on its standard input, and what the harness does is streamed back as it happens. A task's run takes its prompt as a stream of messages rather than a single one, so it can be fed more while it works, as its feeding says.
Its directory, which a system prompt's HARNESS_DIRECTORY stands for, is that of the harness in use: .claude, .codex, or .opencode.

#### Harnesses

The harness in use is the one picked in the [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope): Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode, Claude Code until another is picked. It is remembered for the user, as the [UserPreferencesScope](../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope) says, not for a project. Every run the application starts goes to it, the tasks, the questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes and commit messages it writes, and everything else works the same whichever it is. A run already going when another is picked finishes with the harness it started with, and a conversation is only carried on by the harness it began with; the next request with another harness starts a new one.
Each harness is run its own way, streaming what it does as a line of JSON per event, which is read into the same reply, tool calls, usage, and result, whichever harness wrote it:

- Claude Code is `claude -p`, in auto mode, the system prompt given with `--append-system-prompt`, a conversation carried on with `--resume`, and a copy of one with `--fork-session`.
- Codex is `codex exec`, with `--full-auto` and `--json`, the prompt read from its standard input, a conversation carried on with `resume`.
- OpenCode is `opencode run`, with `--format json`, a conversation carried on with `--session`.

Codex and OpenCode take no system prompt of their own, so it is given ahead of the prompt, marked off from it. Neither can carry on a copy of a conversation, so a question asked while another is running starts a new conversation with them instead. The notes and commit messages are written with a small model where the harness can be told one, Claude Code's haiku, and with the harness's default model otherwise.
When the harness picked isn't installed, a run fails saying that it can't be run, as any run that can't be started does.

#### Feeding

A task's run is given its prompt as a stream of messages: Claude Code with `--input-format stream-json`, each message written as a line of JSON on the harness's standard input, which stays open for as long as the run lasts. The run's first message is the task's compiled prompt, as ever, and each message sent to the task after it, from the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope), is written as another.
A message reaches the harness when it finishes what it is doing rather than interrupting it, so a run that is mid-tool-call takes it once that call is over. Each message the harness answers reports its own result, and a result no longer ends the task on its own: the run ends when the harness has reported a result for every message sent to it, at which point its input is closed and the task finishes, in the state of its last result. A run that is stopped closes its input straight away.
Codex's `codex exec` and OpenCode's `opencode run` read a single prompt and can't be fed more while they work, so a task running with either takes its prompt as ever and can't be sent more.
Questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes and commit messages each take a single prompt, as ever.

#### Context

The harness keeps its context between requests instead of starting fresh each time. Tasks share one ongoing conversation, and each task sent carries it on. When the project is opened, tasks carry on the latest conversation in its history. Questions from the Ask tab share a separate conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they carry on the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question asked while another is running carries on a copy of that conversation, so questions running at the same time never write over each other. A conversation is only carried on in the project it began in, each open project keeping its own tasks' and questions' conversations while it is in the background, and if one can't be carried on, the next request starts a new one. Each run applies its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a conversation begun in a different mode. The palette's file search always starts fresh.
A conversation can be left for a new one, from the chat input's New conversation button, as the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) says: the next request starts a new conversation with no context, and the one left is not carried on again, not by a run of it still going, nor by the project's history. Leaving it is kept with the project, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, so a project opened after its tasks' or questions' conversation was left starts a new one too, rather than carrying on the latest conversation in its history, until a run after the reset begins one of its own. How much context a conversation holds is known from what the harness reports with each reply: everything the model was given, cached or not, and what it wrote, as of its latest reply; replies of subagents don't count.

# Prompt Sending Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

How a prompt gets to the harness, whether written in the chat input or sent on the application's behalf.

### Shape

#### Description

A prompt is sent in one of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), with anything attached to it. Sending is never blocked by the harness working.

#### Tasks

A task, a prompt in Code, Chain, or Spec, is sent straight away while the harness is free. While the harness is working, it waits in the [PromptEditor](../index.md#prompt-editor)'s queue instead, in the order it was sent, keeping its mode and attachments, until its turn comes.
When a task is actually sent, the spec is built ahead of it, as the [SpecBuildScope](../../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says, the task showing "Building" until the build is over; then its hidden anchor is compiled and run. It heads the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list) as the latest task, and is saved in the prompt history, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. A prompt that fails to compile or run fails its task, and doesn't stop the queue.

#### Questions

A question, a prompt in Ask, never queues: it runs straight away, even while the harness is working on a task or other questions, joins the questions stacked above the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)'s tabs, and is saved among the questions asked.

#### Sending To ATask

While a task is running, more can be sent to it, as to a terminal session, from the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)'s "Send to task", as it says. What is sent is written as a hidden anchor and compiled like any prompt, its references, attachments, and Slice toggle included, so it can reference the spec, but the spec isn't built first, and its systemPrompt isn't sent, since the run already has the one it began with. It goes to the running task's run as a message of its own, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, and is not a task of its own: it doesn't head the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list), isn't among the previous tasks, and can't be resent. It is shown in the task's output and kept with its record, as the [PromptEditor](../index.md#prompt-editor) says. A message that fails to compile isn't sent, and a notification titled "Could not send to the task" says why, what was typed going back into the input. A message whose task ends before it can be sent is queued instead, as a task, so nothing typed is lost.

#### On The Applications Behalf

Something in the application can send a prompt as if it were written in the chat input and sent from one of its tabs. It goes just the same

##### Way

queued if the harness is busy, shown as a task, and entered in the

history. What is being written in the chat input, and attached to it, is left alone.

#### Resending

A prompt sent before can be sent again, from a Resend button: a small ghost button with a rotating-arrow icon, whose tooltip says it sends the prompt again as it was sent. It sits at the right of the latest task's header, and of the heading of each previous task and previous answer, beside its chevron; clicking it never opens or closes the item.
Resending sends the prompt as it was typed, in the mode it was sent in, with the text that was attached to it, and sliced or not as it was, as though it were sent afresh from the chat input: a task queues while the harness is working, a question runs straight away, and either is compiled anew, against the spec and system prompt as they are now, building the spec first as any task does, and saved in the history as a new task or question. The prompt resent stays where it is. A prompt whose mode isn't known, saved before modes were, is resent from the chat input's selected tab. What is being written in the chat input, and attached to it, is left alone, and so is the Slice toggle.

# Task Table Scope

## How To Build

A TaskTableScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A TaskTableScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Columns

Type, Output, and Status

## Lock

each use

## Collapses

step

## Pitch

A table of rows under a header of named columns, that can grow long and keep growing while it is shown, and stays smooth however long it gets.

## Table

Its header reads Type, Output, and Status.
Each use says whether its table has the lock to the bottom, and whether it starts on.
A use can say its table collapses its steps, which the first row counts as "Show 1 step" or "Show N steps".

## Concept

### Pitch

The output of one run of the harness, as a table of everything it did, filling in as it does it.

### Shape

#### Description

A [TableScope](../table/TableScope.md#table-scope) with Type, Output, and Status columns, with one row per thing the harness did, in order: each piece of reply text, each tool call, and any error. It is the same table wherever a run's output is shown, a task, a question, a previous task or answer, the palette's search for a file, or a run in one of the application's own panels, and each use says where it sits.

#### Types

##### Description

Type is a coloured badge with an icon. Reply text is "Reply", errors are "Error", and a message sent to the run while it works is "Sent". Tool calls are "Files" for Read, Glob, Grep, LS, and NotebookRead; "Edit" for Edit, MultiEdit, Write, and NotebookEdit; "Command" for Bash, BashOutput, KillShell, and KillBash; "Web" for WebFetch and WebSearch; "Agent" for Task and Agent; and "Tool" for anything else.

#### Status

##### Description

A tool call's status is "running", "done", or "failed", and a call still running when the run ends takes the state the run ended in.

#### Replies

##### Description

Reply text is rendered as markdown, with no border around it. What subagents do is left out. If nothing streamed but the harness reports a final result, that result is shown as the reply. A finished run with nothing to show reads "No output."

#### Tool Calls

##### Description

A tool call's Output cell shows its most telling argument. For Files, Edit, Command, Web, and Agent calls the tool's name is left out, since the badge already says what it is; any other tool's name comes first. Arguments other than commands are shown on a single line.

##### Paths

Any path inside the project directory is shown relative to it, and the project directory itself reads `.`.

##### Commands

A command is shown whole, as a syntax-highlighted bash block, and a long one is split across lines at `&&`, `||`, `|`, and `;`, one command per line with the chained ones indented. It never splits inside quotes, command substitutions, brackets, comments, or heredocs.

#### Streaming

##### Description

While the run is under way, the table ends in a waiting row for whatever the harness does next. As soon as a row's type is known, its badge is real, and as soon as its text or argument arrives, that is shown.

##### Raw Output

Until a row has something meaningful to show, its Type cell is a skeleton and its Output cell shows the last three lines of the harness's raw JSON output: muted, monospace, JSON syntax-highlighted, and always three lines tall so the row doesn't jump. Before any output has arrived it reads "Waiting for the harness…".

##### Skeletons

While the input of a Files, Edit, Command, Web, or Agent call is still arriving, its Output cell shows only a skeleton.
A skeleton stands in for a running row only while there is nothing meaningful to show for it. As soon as there is, no skeleton is shown for it at all.

#### Scrolling

##### Description

The table usually has its lock to the bottom, following the run's latest output. While the end of the table is scrolled out of view, raw output that would only change the waiting row redraws nothing. What a row shows that never changes once known, such as a command laid out across lines or a line of raw output highlighted, is worked out once.

#### Collapsed Steps

##### Description

A use can say its table collapses the steps leading up to the answer, once the run is finished, as the [TableScope](../table/TableScope.md#table-scope) collapses rows. The steps are every row up to and including the harness's last tool call; the answer is the rows after it.
A run with no tool calls, or with nothing after its last one, has nothing to collapse and shows whole. A run still under way shows its latest step as usual.

#### Sent

##### Description

A run can be sent more while it works. Each message sent to it is a row of its own, in order among what the harness did, where it was sent. Its Type is a "Sent" badge, and its Output the message's first line, the whole message as it was typed shown on hover. The rows after it are what the harness did in answer, until the next message. A Sent row has no status.
A Sent row is never collapsed among the steps leading up to an answer.

#### Legibility

The output from a realtime agent should be readable and meaningful.
# Prompt Editor

## How To Build

A PromptEditor should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A PromptEditor should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

An interface for sending tasks to a local coding harness like Claude Code, written directly with compiled-on-depand Piton.

### Shape

#### Description

Not a chat. Each prompt sent is a task for the harness, tasks can queue, and each task shows its output until it finishes. There are no message bubbles.

#### Basic Design And Layout

The [MessageList](./message-list/index.md#message-list) fills all available space except for a [ChatInputScope](./chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) along the bottom. From top to bottom it holds the previous tasks row, the header for the latest task, the latest task's output, and the queue.
Before any task has been sent, the space shows a hint instead, which wraps when the view is narrow. It reads "Write a prompt below. Enter adds a line; Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it." or, while no project is open, as the [NoProjectStateScope](../no-project/index.md#no-project-state-scope) says, "Open a project to start prompting."

#### Chat History

[MessageList](./message-list/index.md#message-list)

#### Previous Tasks

Previous tasks are a [HistoryListScope](../../ui/components/history-list/index.md#history-list-scope) along the top of the view, listing every task sent. Its row counts every task but the latest, which heads the view: "No previous tasks", "1 previous task", or "N previous tasks", and each offers Resend. Expanded, the list takes the place of the latest task and its output, and the row reads "Back to the latest task".

#### Header

The latest task heads the view whether or not the harness is working: its status, with a spinner while it is under way, the name of the hidden anchor it was compiled from, and the compiled markdown the harness actually received, which scrolls once it gets tall. Until it has compiled, the prompt as typed is shown instead. At its right, a Resend button sends it again, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. The header shows the prompt the task was sent with, however much is sent to it while it runs; what is sent is shown in its output.
However long the compiled prompt, a prompt sent with its spec slices included, the header lays out only what is in view: the prompt is split into its blocks of markdown, paragraphs, headings, lists, and code blocks, each drawn as it scrolls into view, as the rows of a table are, so a long prompt costs no more to show, scroll, or animate than a short one. The header is as tall as the prompt up to where it starts to scroll.

#### Queue

```
overview: The queue holds the tasks sent while the harness is working, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says, in the order they were sent, and sends them one at a time.
placement: The queue sits along the bottom of the view, below the output and directly above the chat input, with a border along its top. It is not part of the header. A row saying how many prompts are queued, with a chevron, expands to list each queued prompt in order, a line or two of each, with a button to cancel it. Each prompt in the list is numbered, with its number, text, and cancel button vertically centred in its row, and the list scrolls once it gets tall, with a [ScrollbarScope](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar-scope). Each time it is expanded, it opens scrolled to the bottom, on the prompts queued most recently, however it was scrolled when last closed. The same area holds the auto-send switch and the "Send next" button. The queue is shown only while it has anything in it.
cancel: A queued prompt that has not been sent yet can be cancelled, which removes it from the queue for good. A prompt already sent is no longer in the queue.
editing: Each queued prompt in the list also has a button with a pencil icon, before its cancel button, whose tooltip says it edits the prompt. Clicking it edits the prompt in the [ChatInputScope](./chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope), as it says, and its row is highlighted while it is being edited. While it is, it is held where it is: it is never sent, and a queue waiting on it waits, even with auto-send on. Saving the edit puts the new text, in the mode and with the attachments it was saved with, in its place in the queue, saved with the project in place of what it held, then lets the queue go on as before. An edit that can't be saved leaves the prompt as it was, and a notification titled "Could not save the queued prompt" says why. Cancelling the edit, or cancelling the prompt from the list meanwhile, leaves the queue as it was, less that prompt when it was cancelled.
queueingOnPurpose: A prompt queued on purpose from the chat input's send menu, while the harness is free, waits at the end of the queue rather than being sent at once: it goes when "Send next" is clicked, or when the next task is over and auto-send is on.
autoSend: A "Send next automatically" switch picks between sending the next queued prompt as soon as the harness is free, and waiting. It starts switched on. Switching it on while the harness is free sends the next queued prompt straight away. Whenever the harness is free and the queue is not empty, a "Send next" button sends the first queued prompt.
persistence: Queued prompts are saved with the project's data as they are queued, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. The queue is restored the first time the project is opened in a launch; a restored queue waits for "Send next" rather than sending on its own. A queued prompt's file is removed when it is cancelled, or when it is sent, at which point it is saved to the prompt history like any other prompt.
```

#### Projects

Tasks, the queue, and the auto-send switch belong to their project, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says: the view shows the tasks and queue of the project on screen, while those of other open projects carry on in the background. A project's queue only ever sends into that project.

#### Building The Spec

A task builds the spec before it is sent, as the [PromptModesScope](./modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) says, since the task may be the one to fix the spec, its output starting with an error saying the build failed when it does.

#### History

Every task sent is saved in the prompt history with the project's data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, and its record once its run is over. Opening the project, the first time in a launch, brings back every task in order, with its output replayed from that record. The record keeps each message sent to the task while it ran, as typed and as compiled, in its place among the lines the harness printed, so the task comes back as the exchange it was, each message a Sent row followed by what came of it. A task with no record shows as "Not recorded".
Every question asked from the Ask tab is logged the same way, but among the questions instead, so it never comes back as a task. The record is saved when the run is over, and also when the question is closed or replaced while it runs, with as much as the harness had done. A question that fails before it reaches the harness is logged too, with the error in its record.

#### Chat Input

[ChatInputScope](./chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)
# Project Data Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

What the application keeps for a project, kept in the project itself so it survives a restart and travels with the project.

### Shape

#### Description

Everything the application keeps for a project lives in a `.suspense` directory inside the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/index.md#project-directory-scope), created as it is needed. Nothing about a project is kept anywhere else, apart from the draft.

#### Contents

- `history/`: every task sent, as its hidden anchor's source, named by the second it was sent and the anchor's name, and beside it, once its run is over, a `.json` record of the same name holding the compiled userPrompt the harness received, each line the harness printed, each message sent to the task while it ran, in its place among those lines, and any error
- `asks/`: every question asked from the Ask tab, saved the same way as a task but apart from them
- `queue/`: each queued prompt, as its hidden anchor's source, imports included, named so they list in the order they were queued
- `divergence/`: each divergence report, a JSON file named by when it was made
- `system-prompts/`: each mode's system prompt template, a Markdown file named after its mode, code.md, combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md, and the spec-reading prompt injected into them, spec-reading.md
- `commit-notes.json`: the Git panel's commit notes
- `run.json`: the project's run targets, as the [RunTargetsScope](../run-targets/index.md#run-targets-scope) says
- `harness.json`: the last report the harness gave of the skills and agents it has
- `conversations.json`: which conversation of the tasks, and of the questions, was last left for a new one, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, so it isn't carried on again once the project is reopened

The draft, `.suspense-draft.pi`, isn't in `.suspense`: it is the prompt being written, as `piton lsp` is shown it, a document named as if it were in the spec location, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../project-locations/index.md#project-locations-scope) says, so the server resolves its imports.

#### Machine Only

Some of it belongs to one machine rather than to the project: the harness report `.suspense/harness.json`, the queue `.suspense/queue/`, the commit notes `.suspense/commit-notes.json`, the conversations left `.suspense/conversations.json`, whose conversations only this machine's harness knows, and the draft `.suspense-draft.pi` wherever it is, should it ever be written. Git ignores these, so they are never committed. Everything else, the prompt history, the questions, the divergence reports, and the system prompts, is kept with the project.

#### Reading

What can't be read is left out, or shown as missing, rather than stopping the rest from being read.

#### Last Project

When the application starts, it opens the project that was opened most recently, the first of the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/index.md#project-directory-scope)'s recent projects that still holds its piton.config.pi. With none, it starts with no project open.

# GPUI Kit Assets

> [!NOTE]
> **The complete catalog does not make existing applications embed every icon.**
> `Assets` keeps the original 101 component icons. Applications provide additional
> icons through their own `AssetSource`, as before; they do not need to redeclare
> the component icons. Only explicitly registering `AllAssets` embeds all 1,830
> SVGs on native platforms. Depending on the crate or using the shared `IconName`
> alone does not reference every SVG payload.
>
> | Native asset configuration | Embedded SVG data | Binary increase vs. default `Assets` |
> | --- | ---: | ---: |
> | Default component icons (101) | 44.28 KiB | 0 B (baseline) |
> | Default + 2 application icons (103) | 45.04 KiB | +15.19 KiB |
> | Default + 10 application icons (111) | 48.09 KiB | +19.19 KiB |
> | Explicit `AllAssets` (1,830) | 731.45 KiB | +1.02 MiB |
>
> **In this example, adding 10 application icons costs about 19 KiB, not the full
> catalog.** Their SVGs total 3,903 bytes; the measured binary increase is 19,648
> bytes, including the extra source's lookup/list-composition code, metadata and
> alignment. These are not fixed per-icon costs or whole-application sizes.
>
> Measured with Lucide 1.43.0 on Linux x86_64, Rust 1.98.0, `--release`, and stripped
> symbols. Each program uses the same `IconName` lookup and runtime asset path.
> The extra source falls back to `Assets`, and merges, sorts and deduplicates both
> sources' lists. The 10 extras are `Accessibility`, `AlarmClock`, `Archive`,
> `Award`, `Backpack`, `Bike`, `Bird`, `Camera`, `Coffee` and `Compass`; the two-icon
> case uses the first two. SVG complexity, toolchain and source implementation
> change the result.
>
> Binary size is not RAM usage. Selected sources borrow static bytes without a
> copy/cache; actual rendering still allocates for parsing, rasterization and
> render caches. Runtime shared-name lookup can retain a name/path table, and
> Cargo's downloaded package/build artifacts still contain the complete catalog.
> On WASM, `Assets::new(endpoint)` and `AllAssets::new(endpoint)` use the existing
> on-demand CDN loader instead of embedding the complete bundle.

The shared icon names and assets for [GPUI Kit](https://gpui-kit.com), exposed as
`gpui_kit::assets`. The crate depends on GPUI, not GPUI Component, so Base and
alternative presentation layers can use its complete `IconName` catalog.

`gpui_kit::assets::IconName` provides the complete shared catalog without a
Component dependency. `gpui_kit::component::IconName` remains the original
compatibility enum: existing imports, exhaustive matches and `.view(cx)` calls
continue to work without a new trait import. `Icon::new(...)` accepts either
type. A legacy name converts into the shared name with `.into()`.

For the new shared enum, use `Icon::new(name).view(cx)` when a component entity
is needed, or import `gpui_kit::component::IconNameExt` to call `name.view(cx)`.

The catalog contains all 1,818 Lucide 1.43.0 icons plus 12 retained GPUI Kit
icons. `IconName::ALL` enumerates it; names are generated from bundled SVGs
at build time without network access or another crate's source directory.

}

}

// Keep direct `.child(IconName::Search)` usable by every presentation layer.
// Explicit themed sizes and transformations belong to the consumer's Icon.
impl RenderOnce for IconName {

        let text_style = window.text_style();
        svg()
            .path(self.path())
            .flex_shrink_0()
            .size(text_style.font_size.to_pixels(window.rem_size()))
            .text_color(text_style.color)
    }
}

impl From<IconName> for AnyElement {
    fn from(name: IconName) -> Self {
        name.into_any_element()
    }
}
